haida_master_carpenter.name: Carve the dugout cedar canoe
haida_master_carpenter.notes: The supernatural shipwright who builds dugout canoes; in the Skidegate cycle he repeatedly fashions and rejects split canoes until he perfects the craft before going to war with South-East Wind.

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, BAE Bulletin 29 (1905), 'Master-Carpenter and South-East'

haida_master_carpenter.name: Shape and order the things of the world by carving
haida_master_carpenter.notes: As culture-hero artificer, he gives form to the made world; in tellings overlapping the Raven complex he carves and fits together the fabric of houses, canoes and tools.

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Contributions to the Ethnology of the Haida, Jesup North Pacific Expedition (1905)

hattic_kasku.name: Guarantor of oaths as the moon in heaven
hattic_kasku.notes: As the Anatolian moon-god (cognate of Hurrian Kušuḫ and Luwian Arma), he stands among the celestial witnesses invoked to guarantee oaths and treaties.

sources.reference: Daniel Schwemer, in Reallexikon der Assyriologie, s.v. moon-gods of Anatolia; Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994)

guarani_kuarahy.name: Avenge the slain mother and destroy the man-eating jaguars
guarani_kuarahy.notes: On learning from a bird that the Aña/jaguars had killed his mother Ñande Sy, the Sun-twin leads the slaughter of the monster-jaguars, sparing only a single pregnant female from whom present-day jaguars descend.

sources.reference: León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta (1959); Curt Nimuendajú, Die Sagen von der Erschaffung und Vernichtung der Welt (1914)

haida_raven.name: Steal the daylight (sun, moon and stars) and loose it on the dark world
haida_raven.notes: Raven, by trickery, takes the box in which the light of day is hidden and releases the sun, moon and stars, ending the primordial darkness; the most-told episode of the Haida Raven cycle.

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, BAE Bulletin 29 (1905), the Raven cycle

haida_raven.name: Make Haida Gwaii and the first people from the clamshell
haida_raven.notes: As transformer-creator he is credited with raising Haida Gwaii and coaxing the first humans out of a clamshell on the beach.

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, BAE Bulletin 29 (1905)

haida_djilaqons.name: Bring the founding Eagle-moiety people in canoes
haida_djilaqons.notes: The ancestress from whom (save one northern lineage) the Eagle-moiety Haida descend; tradition has her bring the foundational population to the islands by canoe.

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Contributions to the Ethnology of the Haida, Jesup North Pacific Expedition (1905)
Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994); description of the silver statuette of the war-god holding shield and mace
Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994)

guarani_tupa.name: The thunder and lightning he hurls

sources.reference: León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta (1959); the fourth divine father Tupã Ru Ete as lord of thunder, lightning, rain and the waters
Mahabharata, Drona Parva (the day-13 chariot assault on the Chakravyuha)

hindu_aruna.name: The seven-horsed chariot of Surya he drives

sources.reference: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika, the Garuda-Vinata cycle); Bhavishya Purana (Surya iconography)
Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha and Yuddha Kandas; the name angada denotes the upper-arm ornament
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata installs Rama's padukas on the throne at Nandigrama)

haida_raven.name: The box of daylight (holding sun, moon and stars)

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, BAE Bulletin 29 (1905); the Raven-steals-the-light episode

haida_raven.name: Raven rattle (chief's regalia, with daylight in the beak)

sources.reference: Northwest Coast chief's raven-rattle iconography; cf. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905)

hattic_telipinu.name: The kurša fleece (sheepskin hunting-bag) hung on the eya-tree

sources.reference: The Telipinu Myth (CTH 324); Hittite ritual texts describing the kurša hung from the eyan-tree before the god
Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna, master archer)

Puranic and solar-temple iconography; Stella Kramrisch, The Hindu Temple (1946)
Rigveda (passim); the mother of the Adityas
Rigveda 1.89.10 and passim

hindu_balarama.gloss: he whose weapon is the plough

sources.reference: Bhagavata Purana 10; Vishnu Purana 5

hindu_balarama.gloss: the drawer-together (transferred from Devaki's womb to Rohini)

sources.reference: Bhagavata Purana 10.2
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda

hattic_kasku.gloss: alternative reading of the Hattian moon-god's name

sources.reference: Daniel Schwemer's proposed alternate reading, noted in scholarship on the Hattic moon-god

guarani_tupa.name: Invocation of Tupã in the storm
guarani_tupa.notes: As the divine father of thunder, lightning and rain, Tupã is named in the rolling of the storm; the colonial missions later appropriated the name Tupã to render the Christian God, but in Mbyá cosmology he is the youngest of the four divine fathers, the thunder-and-water power.

sources.reference: León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta (1959)
Branislava Susnik, studies of Guarani religion

herero_ndjambi.name: Thanksgiving invocation of Ndjambi after deliverance
herero_ndjambi.notes: Ndjambi receives no organized cult: his name (held in reverence and not lightly uttered) is invoked in thanksgiving after unexpected good fortune, or in prayer when all other help has failed; the one who dies a natural death is said to be 'taken away by Ndjambi'.

sources.reference: Encyclopedia of African supreme beings; H. Vedder / Luttig on Herero religion

hausa_dan_galadima.name: Bori possession-dance mounting of Dan Galadima
hausa_dan_galadima.notes: The playboy-prince spirit is a favourite of the bori possession-cult; called into a mounted devotee with his praise-music, he is associated with sudden gambling-luck and with the maladies of fever and wasting that the cult both diagnoses and treats.

sources.reference: A. J. N. Tremearne, The Ban of the Bori (1914)
Fremont E. Besmer, Horses, Musicians, and Gods: The Hausa Cult of Possession-Trance (1983)

hausa_inna.name: Bori rite of Inna (Bakar Doguwa) with black sacrifice
hausa_inna.notes: As a senior, dangerous Doguwa spirit who strikes with paralysis, fever and infertility, Inna is treated in the bori cult by initiation and offering; a black chicken or black goat (echoing her name Bakar Doguwa, 'the Black Tall-Woman') is sacrificed to placate her.

sources.reference: A. J. N. Tremearne, The Ban of the Bori (1914)
Fremont E. Besmer, Horses, Musicians, and Gods (1983)

attributes.name: Reddish, dawn-coloured body
attributes.notes: Personified red glow of dawn; depicted ruddy-hued, the herald of Surya who tempers the sun's first rays.

sources.reference: Puranic solar iconography; Stella Kramrisch, The Hindu Temple (1946)

attributes.name: Seated as charioteer before Surya
attributes.notes: Shown crouched at the front of the chariot driving the seven horses of the Sun, as on the Konark and Modhera sun-temples.

sources.reference: Archaeological Survey of India, Konark sun-temple

attributes.name: Fair (white) complexion
attributes.notes: Iconographically pale-skinned, contrasting the dark Krishna; said to be born of a white hair of Vishnu, and worshipped at Puri as the white-faced Balabhadra.

sources.reference: Bhagavata Purana 10.2; Vishnu Purana 5

attributes.name: Multi-hooded serpent (Shesha) above or behind him
attributes.notes: As an incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha/Ananta, he is often shown with a snake-hood canopy.

sources.reference: Vishnu Purana 5.9; standard Vaishnava iconography

attributes.name: Standing upon the back of a lion
attributes.notes: The Hattic-Hittite war-god is depicted standing on a lion (the lion being his pedestal-animal), holding shield and mace.

sources.reference: Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994)
Volkert Haas, Geschichte der hethitischen Religion (1994); the lion-pedestal of the war-god

attributes.name: Feathered flower-crown (jeguaka) jewelled with dew-flowers
attributes.notes: The First Father takes form crowned with the sacred feathered headdress, its flowers shining like drops of dew, emblem of his divinity and of masculine adornment.

sources.reference: León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta (1959), Cap. I
León Cadogan, Ayvu Rapyta (1959): the primeval hummingbird Maino'i feeds and refreshes the First Father as he creates

attributes.name: Enormous prehensile penis coiled about the waist
attributes.notes: Defining attribute of the squat, hairy, copper-skinned wild-man: an oversized prehensile phallus wound several times around his body, the instrument of his forest-fertility and of the abductions and pregnancies blamed on him.

sources.reference: Narciso R. Colmán, Ñande Ypy Kuéra (1929); Dionisio González Torres, Folklore del Paraguay

attributes.name: Giant lizard's body bearing seven dog-like heads
attributes.notes: First-born of the seven; a huge slow-moving lizard surmounted by seven canine heads.

sources.reference: Narciso R. Colmán, Ñande Ypy Kuéra (1929); Dionisio González Torres, Folklore del Paraguay

attributes.name: Eyes that blaze and shoot fire
attributes.notes: Each of the seven heads has eyes that burn like the sun and cast fire, lighting the caverns he haunts as guardian of caves, fruits and hidden riches.

sources.reference: Narciso R. Colmán, Ñande Ypy Kuéra (1929); Dionisio González Torres, Folklore del Paraguay

attributes.name: Great serpent's body with a parrot's head and beak
attributes.notes: Second-born; a giant snake bearing the head and brilliant beak of a parrot, lord and protector of the creatures of the water and the wetlands.

sources.reference: Narciso R. Colmán, Ñande Ypy Kuéra (1929); Dionisio González Torres, Folklore del Paraguay

attributes.name: Antenna-like horns that hypnotize prey
attributes.notes: Third-born; a great horned serpent whose feeler-horns mesmerize his quarry; lord of the open fields and the air, who hoards plunder in his cave.

sources.reference: Narciso R. Colmán, Ñande Ypy Kuéra (1929); Dionisio González Torres, Folklore del Paraguay

attributes.name: Portrait-mask of the Eagle ancestress
attributes.notes: Dzila'qons is a recognized subject of Haida portrait masks and crest art; one of the four monumental supernatural-being masks commissioned for the Haida Gwaii Museum at Skidegate.

sources.reference: Haida Gwaii Museum, Skidegate (the four supernatural-being masks); Haida crest-art tradition

sacredAnimals.name: Salmon (whose runs she releases from the river-heads)

sources.reference: John R. Swanton, Contributions to the Ethnology of the Haida (1905); Creek Woman as matron of fresh water and the salmon

sacredPlants.name: Evergreen eya-tree (eyan)
sacredPlants.notes: An evergreen eya-tree was set up before Telipinu and the kurša fleece hung from it; its perpetual green betokened enduring life and fertility in his ritual.

sources.reference: The Telipinu Myth (CTH 324) and associated Hittite rituals; the eyan-tree with suspended kurša
